title: Cryo-ET comparison of the hierarchical ultrastructure of silkworm, spider, and artificial silk fibers

paper_content.abstract:
Spider and silkworm silks are renowned for their exceptional mechanical properties, which arises from their
ultrastructural organization. However, this architecture remains incompletely understood. Here, we apply cryo-
electron tomography to examine the hierarchical organization of silkworm, spider, and artificial silks. In
silkworm silk, we observe nanofibrils of ~3.6 nm in diameter, interconnected by abundant bridges and
representing the smallest fibrillar features currently accessible by cryo-ET. These nanofibrils align with the fiber
axis and are organized into a herringbone pattern, with stacked layers building the micron-scale filament. Spider
silk displays densely packed nanofibrils with near-perfect axial alignment and minimal voids. In contrast,
silkworm silk shows regionally heterogeneous gaps, whereas artificial silk lacks the ordered packing
characteristic of natural materials. These observations provide a structural basis for understanding silk formation
and may guide future biomimetic fiber design.
paper_content.introduction:
Natural silk, primarily derived from silkworms and spider major ampullate gland, exhibits excellent mechanical
properties, including high tensile strength and toughness. This gives them not only tensile strength comparable to that
of high-performance steel or Kevlar but also exceptional toughness1-3. For millennia, silk has been prized in textiles
for its smooth texture, luster, and strength. More recently, due to its extraordinary mechanical properties, as well as
biocompatibility, biodegradability, and eco-friendly manufacturing methods, silk fibers are becoming a candidate
material for biomedical engineering4-7, flexible electronic wearables8,9 and data storage medium10, attracting
increasing attention11-20.

The superior mechanical properties of silkworm silk and spider silk are closely tied to their ultrastructure,
specifically the morphology, size and hierarchical assembly of the fundamental building blocks within the fibers.
Decades of research have focused on understanding how silk proteins, stored in a soluble state in the silk glands,
transform into insoluble solid fibers with distinct mechanical properties. Two primary models, liquid crystal
spinning21-25 and micellar spinning26, have sought to explain this process. The liquid crystalline model proposes
that spinning dopes in the spider gland and duct adopt a nematic phase, characterized by rod-like structures that
are considered aggregates of spherical silk
proteins21,23. In contrast, the micelle model suggests that natural silk
fibroin (NSF) forms micelles, approximately 100–200 nm in diameter, in solution due to its amphiphilic primary
sequence26,27. As the NSF concentration increases, these micelles coalesce into globules ranging from 0.8 to 15
µm in diameter, which subsequently align under shear forces to form fibers26,28.

Despite these models, the precise structural units and assembly process of silk proteins in silk glands remain
largely elusive. Our recent studies29 have shown a multi-scale controllable self-assembly spinning mechanism
based on the NSF in silkworm spinning dope, suggesting that flexible nanofibrils may represent key building
elements, approximately 4 nm in diameter, rather than the previously suggested micellar structure26,28,30,31 or rod-
like structure formed by aggregation of globular fibroin molecules23. Within the silk glands, these fibroin
nanofibrils initially exhibit random orientation, but intriguingly, they align into a herringbone pattern in the
anterior silk gland near the spinneret. This raises questions about whether this ordered structure persists in the
final silk fibers or undergoes further transformation during the spinning process. Thus, it is essential to
investigate the ultrastructure of silk fibers for a comprehensive understanding of the spinning process.

In addition to natural silk fibers, artificial silks have attracted increasing interest due to their potential for scalable
production and customizable properties. Artificial silk is typically produced by regenerated silk fibroin16,32 or
recombinant silk proteins13-15,18,20 using techniques such as wet spinning13,15,16,18-20,32, dry spinning31,33,
electrospinning14, interface wiredrawing34 or microfluidic spinning35,36. These processes aim to fabricate
artificial silk fibers with structures and properties comparable to those of natural silk, but the properties of
resulting artificial silk fibers are particularly influenced by factors such as protein sequence, spinning dope
concentration, flow rate, humidity, post-spin stretching, buffer composition, etc11,12,33. The ultrastructure within
artificial silk is even less understood. Understanding these structural discrepancies is crucial for improving
artificial silk production and bridging the performance gap between synthetic and natural materials.

Investigating the ultrastructure of silk fibers from the atomic to the macroscopic scales remains a major challenge.
At the atomic level, previous studies using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, neutron scattering
and solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance have established that silk is a semicrystalline polymer. Its crystalline
regions are primarily composed of β-sheets formed by polyalanine, contributing to silk's strength, while the
amorphous regions, rich in glycine, provide the toughness of the silk fibers37-41. However, a consensus on the
hierarchical structure of silk from the nanoscale to the macroscale is still lacking. Various models based on
atomic force microscope (AFM)42-47, scanning electron microscope (SEM)48 and Anderson light localization49
suggest the presence of nanofibrils with diameters ranging from 20 to 220 nm. Nevertheless, techniques like
transmission X-ray microscopy50 and ultramicrotomy51 have failed to detect nanofibrils, with some studies
indicating silk fibers consist of spherical units, 10-200 nm in diameter, the size of which varies depending on the
type of silk26,30,51-53. Neutron scattering and small-angle XRD40,54 suggest a long-range organization in silk fibers,
although its nature and relationship to the protein sequence remain unclear.

Despite significant progress, many aspects of the supramolecular structure and assembly process of silk remain
unresolved. One major challenge is the lack of suitable techniques for studying the native structure of silk fiber
in vivo. Furthermore, conventional sample preparation methods, such as chemical fixation, dehydration, resin-
embedding and heavy metal staining, often introduce artifacts that result in overly condensed structures,
obscuring the fundamental units of silk. The intrinsically dense structure of silk further complicates efforts to
achieve its high-resolution ultrastructural characterization.

In this study, we combined cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milling with state-of-the-art cryo-electron
tomography (cryo-ET) to investigate the ultrastructure of force-drawn silk fibers from silkworms, spiders, and
that of artificial silk. Cryo-FIB is a cutting-edge technique used to prepare high-quality samples for structural
and ultrastructural analysis, particularly in the context of cryo-ET. This method preserves the native structure,
enables high-resolution imaging by producing ultra-thin sections, and minimizes artifacts typically associated
with conventional sample preparation methods. Our study uncovered the morphological and hierarchical
structure of fibroin within silk fibers with unprecedented level. The results revealed that the fundamental
structural unit of silk is nanofibrils approximately 3.6 nm in diameter, which share the same morphology as those
found in the silk gland. These nanofibrils are arranged in parallel along the fiber axis, forming a herringbone
pattern. Multiple layers of this herringbone pattern stack to form the final micron-scale fiber, indicating that the
herringbone pattern formed near the spinneret remains stable during fiber formation. In spider silk, a more
condensed structure adorned with nanofibrils is clearly observed, with their long axes tightly aligned in parallel
along the flow direction, leaving no visible gaps. In contrast, silkworm silk exhibits larger, regionally varying
gaps between nanofibrils, while artificial silk lacks the highly ordered arrangement found in natural silks. In
summary, gaining a deeper understanding of silk's ultrastructure provides valuable insights into replicating and
improving upon the natural spinning processes of silkworms and spiders, guiding the development of polymer-
based materials with tunable properties.
paper_content.results:
Structure of fibroin extracted from silk glands of silkworm
Fibroin, a key component of silk, is understood to exist either as a spherical macromolecular complex with a
molecular weight of up to 2.4 MDa, composed of a fibroin heavy chain, light chain, and P25 in a molar ratio of
6:6:155, or as a rod-like structure formed by the elongation and aggregation of globular fibroin23,30,52. In this study,
NSFs were extracted from the lumen of posterior silk gland of silkworms. Gel filtration chromatography and 4-
16% SDS-PAGE analysis showed that NSFs are a macromolecular complex formed by the fibroin heavy chain,
light chain, and P25 subunits (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Interestingly, 3-16% BN-PAGE analysis showed two
distinct bands for freshly extracted NSFs, with higher molecular weight bands gradually transforming into lower
molecular weight bands upon the addition of amphipol. This transformation displayed a dose-dependent
relationship with amphipol concentration (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Metal shadowing analysis confirms that
(Supplementary Fig. 1c-e).

For improved sample uniformity, NSFs were treated at a 1:6 molar ratio for 72 hours (Supplementary Fig. 1b)
and rapidly frozen via plunge-freezing. Cryo-ET revealed that NSFs exhibit typical fibrous protein
characteristics, displaying high flexibility with a diameter of 4.0 ± 0.6 nm and a length of 32.7 ± 16.4 nm (mean
± SD) (Fig. 1, a-c). While the diameters of individual nanofibers were highly uniform, the lengths varied
significantly (Fig. 1c). Subtomogram averaging further revealed that fibroin nanofibers appear as a string of
beads structure (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Fig. 2), and metal ions are essential for maintaining this structure29.

Most studies suggest that the spherical structures in nanofibrils represent either fibroin monomers 23,56 or fibroin
aggregates26,30,31,52,57-59. The fibroin heavy chain consists of 12 repeat sequences and 11 linker sequences, with
the repeat sequences containing a high proportion of GAGAGS and GAGAGY motifs that govern the mechanical
properties of silk fibers, and the linker sequences showing high conservation (Supplementary Fig. 3), which
provides evidence for the concerted evolution of silk protein genes60,61. Since AlphaFold 3 can only predict
polypeptide structures up to 5000 amino acids62, we deleted one repeat and one linker sequence from fibroin
heavy chain (Δ2303-2621) to predict its structure. The results indicated that the fibroin heavy chain (Δ2303-
2621) can fold into a spherical structure measuring approximately 10.6 nm × 10.7 nm × 15.1 nm (Fig. 1e), which
is significantly larger than the 4 nm × 4 nm × 4 nm spherical structures observed in nanofibrils (Fig. 1d). Due to
the absence of homologous sequences, the three-dimensional (3D) structure of fibroin heavy chain predicted by
AlphaFold 3 lacked accuracy and confidence. Therefore, while this model does not accurately represent the true
structure of the fibroin heavy chain, it provides a useful reference for estimating the size of fibroin. That is, if
the fibroin heavy chain is folded into a tight spherical structure, its size is approximately 10.6 nm × 10.7 nm ×
15.1 nm, while the actual spherical structure in individual nanofibrils is much smaller than predicted size.
Therefore, we hypothesize that the smaller globular structures observed in nanofibrils represent individual
domains formed by segments of the fibroin molecule. Unfortunately, due to the flexibility of NSF nanofibrils,
obtaining high-resolution 3D structures through single-particle reconstruction remains challenging.
Consequently, it is still unclear how many spherical domains an individual fibroin nanofibril consist of.

Structure of fibroin in silkworm silk
To determine whether the morphology of NSF nanofibrils changes during silk formation, we reconstructed the
morphology and organization of silk proteins within silk fibers from third-instar silkworm. Using cryo-FIB
milling, the lamella with the thickness ≤ 100 nm were qualified for decreasing the overlapping signal in the 2D
image during the data collection (Supplementary Fig. 4, a-b). The lamella was transferred to a Titan Krios cryo-
electron microscope (cryo-EM) for data collection (Supplementary Fig. 4c). In the fibroin region inside the silk
fibers，nanofibrils are oriented parallel to the fiber axis, with consistent widths, whereas the sericin region lacked
a distinct nanofibril structure (Fig. 2, a-b, Supplementary Fig. 4d). Interestingly, an unknown macromolecular
structure was observed in the sericin region (Fig. 2b), but this macromolecular is absent in the sericin region of
cocoon silk. It is therefore speculated that this structure might be a specific macromolecule expressed during the
early larval stage of silkworms. Despite the overall parallel arrangement of nanofibrils in the fibroin regions, we
found that the nanofibril distribution was uneven, with tightly packed areas and looser regions (Fig. 2, a-b). The
imperfect parallel arrangement of nanofibrils resulted in gaps within the silk fibers, which could be a contributing
factor to fiber fractures during stretching63,64. In the densely packed areas, nanofibrils were laterally associated,
forming bridges (Fig. 2, c-f) that may be relevant to mechanical coupling between neighboring nanofibrils.

A small set of nanofibrils were picked from the tomogram, aligned, and averaged (Supplementary Fig. 5a), We
found that the fibroins in silk also appeared as nanofibrils with diameters of 3.6 ± 0.8 nm and lengths of 81.9 ±
38.5 nm (mean ± SD) (Fig. 2, g-h), morphologically similar to those extracted from silk glands in vitro (Fig. 1d).
The results indicate that the morphology of fibroin nanofibrils appears broadly similar as they move through the
lumen of silk gland to form silk fibers. Our measurements likely overestimate nanofibril length, as tightly
connected nanofibrils cannot always be distinguished. Notably, such small diameters for nanofibrils have not
been previously reported for silk.

Structure of silk protein in spider silk and artificial silk
There are significant differences in mechanical properties between silkworm silk and spider silk, particularly
spider dragline silk, which surpasses silkworm silk and even outperforms the best synthetic fibers like Kevlar65.
Using metal shadowing detection, we found that the morphology of natural spidroin (NSP) in the lumen of the
spider’s major ampullate gland (Araneus ventricosus) closely resembled the fibroin of silkworms, appearing as
a string of beads (Fig. 3, a-c). However, the molecular weight of NSP was lower than that of silkworm NSF (Fig.
3d). Recent studies have shown that the silk from major ampullate glands of spiders contain 18 proteins66.

To further investigate the relationship between the ultrastructure of animal silk and its mechanical properties, we
manually pulled fresh silks from the spider and used cryo-FIB milling to prepare lamella ≤ 100 nm thick
(Supplementary Fig. 6, a-c). Then, the samples were transferred to a cryo-EM for high-resolution 3D imaging
(Fig. 3e, Supplementary Fig. 6d). Cryo-EM revealed numerous nanofibrils arranged parallel to the long axis of
the spider silk fibers. Unlike the loose arrangement of nanofibrils in silkworm silk, the nanofibrils in spider silk
were tightly packed and well-oriented with no visible gaps (Fig. 3f), resulting in a much denser fiber structure
with higher nanofibril density compared to silkworm silk (Supplementary Fig. 7a). This tight packing may
explain why spider silk exhibits superior mechanical properties over silkworm silk.

We also prepared artificial silk fibers using the interface wiredrawing method34 (Supplementary Fig. 8, a-b) and
obtained lamella ≤ 100 nm thick via cryo-FIB milling (Supplementary Fig. S8, c-d). In striking contrast, although
both natural and artificial silk are composed of NSF, artificial silk exhibited minimal nanofibril orientation and
a non-uniform phase distribution (Fig. 3h, Supplementary Fig. 8e). These findings suggest that the buffer
composition during spinning significantly affects the orientation degree and density of the nanofibrils within silk
fibers, and these factors play a crucial role in determining their mechanical properties.

Structural organization of silkworm silk
To investigate whether silk fibers contain ordered structures similar to or higher than the herringbone pattern29
observed near the spinneret in the anterior silk gland，we introduced a deep learning strategy-based method
(REST) to establish the relationship between low-quality and high-quality density, applying this knowledge to
restore signals in cryo-ET (Supplementary Fig. 5b)67. The results show that this method improves the signal-to-
noise ratio of tomographic slices and reduces some artifacts caused by the excessive density of silks and the
missing data region in the 3D reconstruction of sample (missing wedge) (Fig. 4, a-b). Notably, we observed
numerous regularly arranged dot-like structures in the XZ view of the silk fibers (Fig. 4, a-b, bottom). By tracking
each dot along the y axis, we determined that each dot corresponds to a nanofibril, which were densely stacked
on the YZ view (Fig. 4, c-d). This arrangement is consistent with the herringbone patterns found near the
spinneret in the anterior silk gland (Fig. 4e)29. Previous studies29,68 identified an axis within the herringbone
pattern, possibly a pseudo-axis formed by interactions involving the N-terminal domain of the fibroin heavy
chain of fibroin. In our experiments, we observed both tightly connected regions and blank regions within the
same herringbone pattern. Interestingly, a distinct axis perpendicular to the nanofibrils was also evident in the
blank regions of the herringbone pattern (Supplementary Fig. 9a), indicating that there may be other proteins
involved in the formation of the herringbone pattern.

Recent studies propose that the herringbone patterns of fibroin may actually resemble a 3D bottlebrush
structure68. Statistical analyses of the distances between points along the z-axis and x-axes revealed that the
spacing between points along the z-axis is significantly smaller and more uniform than that along the x-axis
(Supplementary Fig. 7b). This finding indicates that the nanofibrils within the silk are anisotropically arranged
rather than simply stacked in parallel. Such an arrangement contributes to enhancing the mechanical properties
of the material69. Moreover, they are organized into a herringbone pattern, where multiple layers of this
herringbone pattern are stacked along the x-axis to ultimately form micro-sized silk fibers (Fig. 4f). Obviously,
the final microscale fiber does not exist as a compressed bundle of aligned nanofibrils, and no higher-order
organization was observed beyond the herringbone pattern. This finding suggests that the herringbone pattern,
formed near the spinneret in the anterior silk gland, remains intact throughout silk fiber formation and is not
replaced by more complex arrangements. Notably, the anisotropic arrangement likely affects the mechanical
properties of silk fibers in the x and z directions.
paper_content.methods:
Ethical Statement
No ethical approval was required for this study, as silkworms (Bombyx mori) and spiders (Araneus
ventricosus) are not subject to institutional animal care and use regulations.

Experimental animal preparation
Silkworms (Bombyx mori) were reared to the third larval stage at room temperature, fed a diet of mulberry leaves.
Twenty adult Araneus ventricosus spiders (body length 1.1-1.7 cm) were collected from the wild in Sichuan and
Beijing, China, between August and October. The spiders were housed individually in separate containers and
provided with moths and water.

Preparation of natural silk fibroin, natural spidroin, and cryo-vitrification
Silkworm larvae were reared at room temperature until reaching the early wandering stage, after which they
were frozen using liquid nitrogen and stored at -80 ºC. Silk glands were dissected from the frozen silkworms,
and the cells on the surface of the posterior of middle silk gland (PMSG) were manually peeled off using forceps.
Then, the spinning drop was transferred to the extraction buffer (50 mmol·L-1 NaCl, 50 mmol·L-1 Bis-Tris, 0.5
mmol·L-1 EDTA, pH 7.5) to dissolve the NSF, resulting in a NSF solution. NSF solution was mixed with
amphipol in extraction buffer at a mass ratio of 1:6. After incubation at 4ºC for 72 h, 3 μL of the mixture was
loaded onto a glow-discharged holey grid (GIG, 1.2/1.3, Au) and vitrified by flash-plunging into liquid ethane
using a Vitrobot Mark IV (FEI, USA). Blotting time, force level and humidity were set to be 7 s, 0 and 100%,
respectively.

Adult spiders were anesthetized at 4℃ for 30 min and then dissected on ice to isolate the major ampullate glands.
The silk glands were rinsed three times with phosphate buffered saline (PBS), and the outer epithelial cell layer
was carefully removed using fine forceps. The gel-like spinning dope was gently extracted and transferred into
PBS to prepare the NSP solution.

Biochemial analysis of natural silk fibroin and natural spidroin
The homogeneity and composition of NSF were assessed by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) and sodium
dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). SEC was performed using a Superose 6
increase 3.2/300 column (GE Healthcare, USA). Protein fractions were subsequently analyzed by SDS-PAGE
and visualized by Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining.

The component of NSP was examined by SDS-PAGE. A homemade linear gradient SDS-PAGE gel (3%-16%)
was prepared using a Hoefer SG 30 gradient maker (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The concentrations of NSF
and NSP were determined by measuring absorbance at 280 nm (A280) with a NanoDrop 2000C
spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

NSF solution was incubated with amphipol (Anatrace, USA) at mass ratio of 1:3, 1:6, 1:9, respectively, at 4ºC.
Following different incubation periods, the samples were mixed with native-PAGE loading buffer (Invitrogen,
USA) and subjected to electrophoresis at 4ºC under the following conditions: 90 V for 30 min, followed by 175
V for 90 min. The gels were stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue. A linear gradient blue native polyacrylamide
gel electrophoresis (BN-PAGE) gel (3%-16%) was cast following Witting’s protocol77, with a Hoefer SG 30
gradient maker (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

Metal shadowing
Metal shadowing was performed following established procedures29,78. For metal shadowing imaging of NSP
and NSF solutions extracted respectively from spider and silkworm, a 5 μL solution (30 μg·mL-1) was applied
to glow-discharged copper grids for 2 min. Excess solution was carefully removed using blotting paper. For
metal shadowing imaging of NSF in silkworm spinning dope and NSP in spider pinning dope, a glow-discharged
copper grid was placed on the spinning dope and gently pressed with tweezers to avoid any artifact formation.
NSF was dehydrated through a graded ethanol series (0, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) for 4 min each step. The samples
were then shadowed with tungsten using a DV-502B high vacuum evaporator (Denton Vacuum, USA) and air-
dried. A tungsten wire (8 cm in length) was clamped between two electrodes at a distance of 3.8 cm, with a
separation of 9.3 cm from the center of the specimen platform. The angle between tungsten wire and the sample
was approximately 10°. The NSF samples were rotated during evaporation for 14.5 min. Transmission electron
microscopy was performed using a Tecnai Spirit (FEI, USA).

Preparation of artificial silkworm silk, force-drawn silk, and cryo-vitrification of silk
samples
Artificial silkworm silk was prepared by the interface wiredrawing as previously described34 with modifications.
Briefly, 3 μL buffer (50 mmol·L-1 Citric acid, 50 mmol·L-1 Bis-tris propane, 16% w/v Polyethylene glycol 3,350,
pH 5.0) was placed on a glass plate, followed by the addition of an equal volume of NSF solution (3 mg·mL-1).
The solutions were quickly mixed with a 10 μL pipette tip, and the resulting artificial silks were immediately
placed on the glow-discharged mesh grids for subsequent analysis.

Fresh silkworm and spider silks were obtained by the forcible silking method. Third-instar silkworms and size-
matched spiders were gently immobilized using adhesive tape and placed under a stereomicroscope. Silk fibers
were then carefully drawn from the spinnerets using fine-tipped tweezers and immediately transferred onto glow-
discharged mesh grids. Third-instar larvae were selected due to their relatively small silk diameter (~3–5 μm),
which facilitates cryo-vitrification.

To ensure the physiological relevance of the fibers studied, the reeling speed was manually controlled to match
the natural spinning rates of silkworms (4-15 mm s-1) and spiders (10-20 mm s-1)79. To prevent dehydration, 3
μL of distilled water was added to the grid prior to silk application. Excess liquid was blotted with Whatman
filter paper for 6 s, and then the grids were rapidly plunge-frozen into liquid ethane using an EM GP system
(Leica Microsystems, Germany). Vitrified grids were stored in liquid nitrogen until further used.

Cryo focused ion beam milling and Cryo-ET data acquisition
Cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milling was performed using a Helios NanoLab 600i Dual Beam SEM
(Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), as previously described80. The goal was to prepare lamellae with a final
thickness of ≤ 100 nm. Frozen grids were transferred with the cryo-transfer shuttle into the SEM chamber via a
Quorum pp3000T cryo-transfer system (Quorum Technologies, UK) at -180℃. During milling, the angle
between the FIB and the silk surface was maintained at 5°- 10°, with milling performed from both sides to create
vitrified silk lamellae. The ion beam accelerating voltage was set at 30 kV, and the current ranged from 0.43 nA
(rough milling) to 10 pA (fine milling). The fine lamellae had a thickness of less than 100 nm.

Cryo-ET data acquisition was carried out using a Titan Krios transmission electron microscope fitted with a K2
detector. Overview tilt series of silks lamellae were acquired under a magnification of ×105,000, resulted in a
physical pixel size of 1.36 Å, under counting mode. Before data collection, the pre-tilt of the sample was
determined visually, and the pre-tilt was set to be 10° or -9° to match the pre-determined geometry caused by
loading grids. And the tilt range were set to be between -60° to +40° for -10° pre-tilt or -40 to +60° for +10° pre-
tilt, with a 3° step, resulting in 33 tilts and 99 electrons per tilt series. The slit width was set to be 20 eV, with the
refinement of zero-loss peak after collection of each tilt series, and nominal defocus was set to be -3.5 to -4.5 μm.
Fro the fibroin extracted from silk glands, the tilt range were set to be between -55° to +55° with a 3° step,
resulting in 35 tilts and 115 electrons per tilt series. All tilt series used in this study were collected using a dose-
symmetry strategy-based beam-image-shift facilitated acquisition scheme, by in-house developed scripts within
SerialEM software. The rest of the collection details are consistent with those mentioned above and are
summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

Tomogram reconstruction and sub-volume averaging of the fibroin
Motion correction and contrast transfer function (CTF) estimation were carried out in Warp; tilt series alignment
was carried out in IMOD 4.8.49 and AreTomo 2. For the fibroin extracted from silk glands, 77 tomograms were
binned 4 and apply the deconvolution method in Warp to denoise in order to facilitate the particle picking. To
pick filaments, CrYOLO 1.6.081 was employed to detect the straight filaments in the XY planes of the tomograms.
These segments were extracted with a box size of 40 pixels (218 Å) using Warp. The reference was used a
featureless cylinder using Dynamo 1.1.332. The sub-volumes were then aligned and classified using RELION
4.0. This averaged structure has an estimated resolution of 24 Å based on the ‘gold-standard’ FSC with 0.143
criterion. The details see supplementary Fig. 2.

For the fibroin within fibers, due to the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in lamella, tomograms were reconstructed
using a SIRT-like filter and binned 2, as implemented in IMOD 4.8.49. Particles picking was performed using
CrYOLO 1.6.0 on the filtered tomograms. These segments were extracted with a box size of 90 pixels (245 Å)
using RELION 3.0. The reference was used a featureless cylinder using Dynamo 1.1.332. The sub-volumes were
then aligned and classified using RELION 3.0. This averaged structure has an estimated resolution of 22 Å based
on the ‘gold-standard’ FSC with 0.143 criterion. The details see supplementary Fig. 5a.

Restoring the tomograms by deep learning
Due to the dense arrangement of silk fibers and the presence of a significant missing wedge effect 3D especially
in XZ plane, we employed the REST method67 for tomogram restoration. First, we generated a ground truth by
randomly distributing the averaged map (many fibers) to densely arrange in the particle box. Then employing
random rotations and shifts (high-quantity datasets), noise and missing wedge artifacts were then added to the
ground truth to form the low-quantity datasets. These data were paired and then were used as training pairs for
REST training. The trained model was subsequently utilized to recover the raw tomograms from the weighted
back-projection (WBP) reconstruction. The details see supplementary Fig. 5b.

Measurement and Visualization
Visualization and figure generation were performed in UCSF ChimeraX v1.3 and IMOD 4.8.49. The diameter
and length of fibroin nanofibrils were measured manually using the measure tool in IMOD 4.8.49 and Fiji 2.32.
To analyze the density of spider and silk fibers, we projected the same number of XY slices into a single 2D
projection keep the same volume. The resulting projection was then binarized, and the proportion of the fibers
in space was quantified by calculating the ratio of white pixels (representing fibers) to the total number of pixels
in the projection.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, the authors utilized cryo-FIB milling and cryo-electron tomography to investigate and compare the structures of silk fibers from the silkworm, spider, and artificial silks. The results revealed previously unknown structural details, including the fundamental structural unit and arrangement, and provided new insight into the structural basis underlying the differences in the mechanical properties of the silkworm silk fibers and spider silk fibers. The manuscript focuses on an interesting topic that may attract readers from various scientific backgrounds. The data and analysis are solid. The manuscript The manuscript is well-organized and clearly written. I enjoyed reading it and think it is almost ready to be published as is in Nature Communication.
I have only some minor suggestions for the authors to consider.
The manuscript studied and compared the structural details of silk fibers from silkworms, spiders, as well as artificial silks. The introduction provided background information about previous structural studies on silkworm silks and spider silks, but not artificial silks. It would be helpful to provide some brief background information about artificial silks, e.g., how they are made and their differences compared to natural silks if known. The structural difference between silkworm silks and spider silks is used to explain the better mechanical properties of spider silk fibers compared to that of the silkworm. While the authors also studied and revealed the structural difference between natural spider silk and artificial silk, can the structural difference be linked to the difference between natural spider silk and artificial silks?
Page 6, Line 204: “(Fig. 4, a b, bottow)” should be “(Fig. 4, a b, bottom)”
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The paper titled “Cryo-ET Analysis Unveils the Minimum Structural Unit and Hierarchical Ultrastructure of Silk Fibers in Silkworm and Spider” describes the ultrastructure of silkworm silk, spider silk, and artificial silk analyzed using cryo-electron tomography. I find such type of work interesting and important for the field of silk biomaterials. It is evident that the authors have put significant effort into acquiring remarkable images using cryo-electron microscopy.
Below, I outline points that could be clarified to improve the paper:
1. Title and Main Message: I believe the title does not accurately reflect the paper's main message and should be revised accordingly. The primary finding, as stated in the abstract, is the identification of differences in the arrangement of nanofibrils among spider silk fibers, silkworm silk fibers, and artificial silk fibers: “In spider silk, a dense structure featuring nanofibrils is clearly visible, with their long axes tightly aligned parallel to the flow direction, leaving no discernible gaps. In contrast, silkworm silk exhibits larger, regionally varying gaps between nanofibrils, while artificial silk lacks the highly ordered arrangement characteristic of natural silks.” (Page 1, lines 24-27). In previous work from the same group/corresponding author (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scib.2023.12.050, also listed in this manuscript as reference 29), the smallest fibrillar unit of approximately 4 nm arranged in a herringbone pattern was reported. Thus, my understanding is that the finding of this work is not a structural unit or a “new pattern,” but rather the differences between the three types of silk. If this is correct, then the title should be changed accordingly, and the abstract should emphasize this point.
2. Methodological Concerns: I am confused by the authors' use of various manipulative methods while simultaneously claiming to operate under purely native conditions where the protein remains unchanged. May be some details were not provided/mentioned? The authors should explain this point, specifically addressing the following:
o Why they applied shear to a shear-sensitive protein and concluded that the protein remained intact.
o Why they added an additional polymer without explaining how they differentiate between the protein and the polymer.
o Why they froze the entire silk gland and how they prevented ice nucleation in this process.
o How they utilized FIB milling and managed to avoid graphitization, considering that silk has low thermal conductivity and may burn even under cryo-FIB conditions.
Co-reviewer:
Overall, I find the paper interesting, and it is clear that significant work and effort have gone into acquiring these results. It presents important findings regarding the size and morphology of silk nanofibrils under different conditions. The use of FIB to create lamellae for TEM imaging is a crucial point, as it emphasizes their effort to maintain the native structure of silk fiber nanostructures.
However, I am not fully convinced that the results are reliable. The bottom line is that they did not measure any material in its native state; they consistently altered it in some way. Even the silk fibers used were forced reeled from the animal. Additional comments can be found throughout the main text and in the methods section.
I strongly disagree with many of the sample preparation choices made by the authors. Most of the techniques employed are likely to change and disrupt the native structure and state of the protein. Bulk freezing, dehydration with ethanol, and the addition of other polymers to the fibroin solution are known to alter fibroin structure and conformation. At the very least, these methods do not represent the native forms of the protein found inside the silk gland.
Furthermore, from my personal experience, it is essential for the authors to provide proof that the silk fibers were not damaged during FIB milling. Even under gentle milling settings and cryogenic conditions, the protein can change structure and heat up significantly.
Specific Comments:
• Page 3, line 108: Applying shear and flow to a shear-sensitive protein is inadvisable.
• Page 4, line 115: If another polymer (amphipol) is added to the sample, how can the authors determine what they observe under the TEM microscope? Is it fibroin or the second polymer? How can they ensure that the second polymer does not alter the fibroin structure or macrostructure?
• Page 4, line 115: 72 hours is a lengthy time to store NSF; the protein structure can be completely altered in that time.
• Page 4, line 147: Are they discussing artificially spun fibers? Is it forced spinning from silkworms? This should be clarified. Why didn't they use natural silk fibers? What is a "molted silkworm"?
• Page 4, line 148: Every FIB lamella preparation of silk needs to be validated with proof that it was not carbonized (e.g., through EDS or diffraction). Silkworm silk fibers have very low thermal conductivity, so during FIB milling, they accumulate energy and can reach high temperatures (>1000°C), leading to pyrolysis and carbonization.
• Page 5, line 161: They barely discuss these bridges. What are their diameters? What do they believe they are composed of?
• Page 5, lines 166-168: This statement is incorrect. Multiple studies have shown that the protein undergoes significant changes along the silk gland.
• Page 6, lines 211-212: I do not understand how they interpret the "perpendicular axis" and how it correlates with the macro- fiber structure.
• Page 9, line 311: This freezing process destroys the samples! Freezing such large samples results in ice crystal formation, which forces the sample into an unnatural morphology. Additionally, ice crystal formation exerts shear on the silk proteins, altering their structure and fibrillation.
• Page 9, line 314: This purification process involves passing the samples through porous scaffolds and applying high shear to the proteins, significantly changing their native non-fibrillated state.
• Page 9, line 328: Why did the authors add amphipol? Do they understand what impact it will have on fibroin?
• Page 9, line 329: Again, 72 hours is a long time to store NSF and expect it to remain unchanged.
• Page 10, line 334: How did they obtain spider silk proteins? This information is not mentioned.
• Page 10, lines 338-339: The authors state that NSF has been dehydrated in ethanol… WHY? Dehydration with ethanol will completely alter the protein structure!
• Page 10, line 348: Why did they add the buffer? Can't they spin it without buffer? It is NSF; they should be able to spin it easily.
• Page 10, line 352: “Forced silking” will also change the structure!
• Page 10, line 358: Everything done using FIB milling needs to be checked to ensure that the material has not been altered due to thermal effects caused by the beam. Even under gentle milling settings and cryogenic conditions, silkworm silk fibers can heat up and form graphene structures. To ensure this is not the case, they should use EDS to check the elemental composition of the lamellae and/or perform electron diffraction.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to reviewers
Manuscript ID: NCOMMS-24-81232
Title: Cryo-ET Analysis Unveils the Minimum Structural Unit and Hierarchical
Ultrastructure of Silk Fibers in Silkworm and Spider
Journal: Nature Communications
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors utilized cryo-FIB milling and cryo-electron
tomography to investigate and compare the structures of silk fibers from the silkworm,
spider, and artificial silks. The results revealed previously unknown structural details,
including the fundamental structural unit and arrangement, and provided new insight
into the structural basis underlying the differences in the mechanical properties of the
silkworm silk fibers and spider silk fibers. The manuscript focuses on an interesting
topic that may attract readers from various scientific backgrounds. The data and
analysis are solid. The manuscript is well-organized and clearly written. I enjoyed
reading it and think it is almost ready to be published as is in Nature
Communications.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of our research.
The comments are valuable and very helpful for us to revise and improve the paper,
and important guidance for our research. We have tried our best to improve the
manuscript and made corresponding revisions, and we hope to meet with approval.
Regarding the comments and suggestions, we would like to respond point-by-point as
follows.
I have only some minor suggestions for the authors to consider.
The manuscript studied and compared the structural details of silk fibers from
silkworms, spiders, as well as artificial silks. The introduction provided background
information about previous structural studies on silkworm silks and spider silks, but
not artificial silks. It would be helpful to provide some brief background information
about artificial silks, e.g., how they are made and their differences compared to
natural silks if known.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion.
We agree that providing background information on artificial silks would improve the
contextual framework of our study, especially since artificial silk is also one of the
key subjects of structural comparison in our work.
To address this, we have added a new paragraph to the Introduction, which outlines
the methods commonly used to fabricate artificial silk (e.g., wet spinning,
electrospinning, and microfluidic spinning), the typical materials employed (e.g.,
regenerated silk fibroin and recombinant silk proteins), and the structural and
mechanical differences between artificial and natural silks reported in the literature.
This addition helps clarify why artificial silk is included as a comparative target in our
study and underscores the significance of elucidating its ultrastructural characteristics.
Revisions in the Manuscript:
A new paragraph has been added to the Introduction (lines 62–72 in the revised
manuscript) as follows:
“In addition to natural silk fibers, artificial silks have attracted increasing interest
due to their potential for scalable production and customizable properties. Artificial
silk is typically produced by regenerated silk fibroin1,2 or recombinant silk proteins3-7
using techniques such as wet spinning1-4,6-8, dry spinning9,10, electrospinning5,
interface wiredrawing11 or microfluidic spinning12,13. These processes aim to fabricate
artificial silk fibers with structures and properties comparable to those of natural silk,
but the properties of resulting artificial silk fibers are particularly influenced by
factors such as protein sequence, spinning dope concentration, flow rate, humidity,
post-spin stretching, buffer composition, etc10,14,15. The ultrastructure within artificial
silk is even less understood. Understanding these structural discrepancies is crucial for
improving artificial silk production and bridging the performance gap between
synthetic and natural materials.”
The structural difference between silkworm silks and spider silks is used to explain
the better mechanical properties of spider silk fibers compared to that of the silkworm.
While the authors also studied and revealed the structural difference between natural
spider silk and artificial silk, can the structural difference be linked to the difference
between natural spider silk and artificial silks?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful and important comment.
Establishing a direct and quantitative link between the structural differences and
mechanical properties of natural spider silk, silkworm silk, and artificial silks is
indeed an important direction, and it remains a key focus of our ongoing research.
In the current study, our primary aim was to resolve long-standing controversies
surrounding the fundamental building blocks and hierarchical ultrastructure of natural
silkworm and spider silks. While we also analyzed the ultrastructure of artificial silks,
we did not measure their mechanical properties in this work, which limits our ability
to directly correlate structural differences with performance differences between
natural and artificial silks.
Nevertheless, the distinct ultrastructural features we observed between artificial and
natural silks strongly suggest that spinning conditions, particularly the composition of
the spinning buffer, play a crucial role in determining the nanostructure of the
resulting fibers (lines 208-210). Since mechanical properties of silks are intimately
tied to their hierarchical structure, we believe these observations provide indirect but
valuable insights into how processing conditions may influence the functionality of
artificial fibers.
Importantly, beyond resolving structural controversies, this study also contributes a
high-resolution methodological framework that can be applied in future investigations
aiming to systematically connect spinning conditions, structural organization, and
mechanical performance of silk fibers. We have added discussion on this point in the
revised manuscript (lines 301–305) to clarify the implication of our findings in the
context of artificial silk development
Revisions in the Manuscript:
A new sentence has been added to the Discussion section (lines 301–305 in the
revised manuscript) as follows:
“Furthermore, a comparison of the ultrastructure between artificial and natural
silkworm silk reveals that, although both are derived from NSFs, differences in buffer
composition during the spinning result in marked variations in fiber ultrastructure.
These structural differences, in turn, significantly influence the mechanical properties
of the resulting silk fibers.”
Page 6, Line 204: “(Fig. 4, a b, bottow)” should be “(Fig. 4, a b, bottom)”
Response: We are particularly grateful to the reviewer for pointing out the mistakes
that we had not noticed.
We have revised “Fig. 4, a b, bottow” as “Fig. 4, a b, bottom” in the revision.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The paper titled “Cryo-ET Analysis Unveils the Minimum Structural Unit and
Hierarchical Ultrastructure of Silk Fibers in Silkworm and Spider” describes the
ultrastructure of silkworm silk, spider silk, and artificial silk analyzed using
cryo-electron tomography. I find such type of work interesting and important for the
field of silk biomaterials. It is evident that the authors have put significant effort into
acquiring remarkable images using cryo-electron microscopy. Below, I outline points
that could be clarified to improve the paper:
Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive and encouraging evaluation of our
work. We are grateful that the reviewer found our study both interesting and
significant for the field of silk biomaterials, and we appreciate your recognition of the
effort invested in acquiring the cryo-EM data.
In response to the reviewer's constructive comments, we have carefully addressed
each of your specific concerns and suggestions in the detailed point-by-point replies.
Where appropriate, we have clarified experimental procedures, expanded explanations
in the Methods and Discussion sections, and revised the manuscript to improve clarity
and rigor.
We believe that these revisions have strengthened our manuscript and enhanced the
clarity of our findings. We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments,
which have helped us improve both the technical details and the overall presentation
of our work.
We hope that the revised version of our manuscript meets the reviewer's expectations
and look forward to the further evaluation.
1: Title and Main Message: I believe the title does not accurately reflect the paper's
main message and should be revised accordingly. The primary finding, as stated in the
abstract, is the identification of differences in the arrangement of nanofibrils among
spider silk fibers, silkworm silk fibers, and artificial silk fibers: “In spider silk, a
dense structure featuring nanofibrils is clearly visible, with their long axes tightly
aligned parallel to the flow direction, leaving no discernible gaps. In contrast,
silkworm silk exhibits larger, regionally varying gaps between nanofibrils, while
artificial silk lacks the highly ordered arrangement characteristic of natural silks.”
(Page 1, lines 24-27). In previous work from the same group/corresponding author
(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scib.2023.12.050, also listed in this manuscript as reference
29), the smallest fibrillar unit of approximately 4 nm arranged in a herringbone
pattern was reported. Thus, my understanding is that the finding of this work is not a
structural unit or a “new pattern,” but rather the differences between the three types of
silk. If this is correct, then the title should be changed accordingly, and the abstract
should emphasize this point.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and constructive
comment regarding the main message and title of our manuscript.
Our study aims to showcase the fundamental building blocks and hierarchical
ultrastructure of silk fibers while also comparing the differences among these silks.
We agree that the comparative analysis of nanofibril arrangements among spider silk,
silkworm silk, and artificial silk fibers represents one of the central findings of this
study. While this work reconfirms the nanofibril unit and herringbone pattern
previously observed16, the current study provides crucial advances in resolving and
comparing these architectures directly in situ across different silk types, under
near-native conditions using cryo-FIB and cryo-ET. Specifically, we directly
visualized the smallest structural units identified to date within the fiber and, for the
first time, discovered their anisotropic arrangement in silkworm silk fibers.
Although the basic structural unit and its arrangement identified in silkworm silk
fibers are consistent with the morphology of silk proteins extracted from the silk
gland and the higher-order structures observed at the terminal region of the anterior
silk gland in our previous work, these features had not previously been reported
within silk fibers. Therefore, this current study provides strong evidence under more
native conditions to address the ongoing debate regarding the fundamental structural
unit in silkworm and spider silk. At the same time, the comparative analysis of
packing density, nanofibril arrangement, and hierarchical organization across the three
silk types constitutes another key contribution of this work, offering new structural
insights into the mechanical performance differences between them.
It is worth mentioning that this study was initially motivated by critiques from some
colleagues who questioned whether the nanofibrillar morphology we previously
observed in silk proteins extracted from the silk gland accurately represented their
native state, raising concerns that extraction conditions might have altered the protein
structure. Moreover, the widely cited micelle model (Jin et al., Nature, 2003) is
primarily based on scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and atomic force microscopy
(AFM) observations, which reveal morphologies that differ substantially from the
nanofibrillar morphology we reported for extracted silk proteins (Song et al., Science
Bulletin, 2024). In light of this, the primary objective of the present study was to
elucidate the ultrastructure structure inside silkworm silk fibers—including the
fundamental structural unit and their arrangement—under near-native conditions, and
to compare these ultrastructures with those found in spider silk and artificial silk
fibers. This work aims to provide important references for deciphering the natural
spinning mechanism and developing biomimetic artificial fibers with superior
comprehensive performance.
On the other hand, due to the highly dense nature of silk fibers, even high-resolution
SEM or AFM techniques struggle to reveal their internal structure clearly,
highlighting the need for more advanced imaging approaches. By employing the
combined cryo-FIB and cryo-ET technique, we made meaningful progress in
addressing this challenge. However, it is regrettable that, due to the extremely dense
structure of spider silk, we were unable to investigate its internal hierarchical
organization in greater detail. Thus, our comparative analysis among these silk fibers
remains relatively preliminary, limited to basic metrics such as packing density. At
present, we are conducting ongoing ultrastructural analyses of seven different spider
silk fiber types, which, given the significant differences in their mechanical properties,
may provide further insights into the internal structural variations among spider silks.
Finally, we sincerely thank the reviewer once again for the valuable suggestions,
which have helped us clarify the main contributions of the current study and provided
important guidance for our future research.
2: Methodological Concerns: I am confused by the authors' use of various
manipulative methods while simultaneously claiming to operate under purely native
conditions where the protein remains unchanged. May be some details were not
provided/mentioned? The authors should explain this point, specifically addressing
the following:
⚫ Why they applied shear to a shear-sensitive protein and concluded that the protein
remained intact.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important concern and appreciate
the opportunity to clarify our experimental approach.
We agree that gel filtration chromatography, like all chromatographic processes,
involve fluid flow and may introduce a certain degree of shear stress, which could, in
principle, influence the morphology of shear-sensitive proteins such as silk fibroin.
However, in our study, the sole purpose of performing gel filtration was to analyse the
homogeneity and composition of NSF. Therefore, even if minor shear-induced
morphological changes occurred during this purification step, they do not affect the
validity of the subunit identification, which was the only purpose of that procedure.
Importantly, we emphasize that gel filtration chromatography or any other
shear-inducing purification steps was not used in the preparation of samples for
vitrification, metal shadowing, or cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET).
We acknowledge that the methodology description in the original manuscript may
have caused confusion. In the revised version, we have clarified the experimental
workflow and explicitly stated which samples underwent gel filtration and for what
purpose, in order to avoid misunderstanding and improve the transparency and
readability of the manuscript (see materials and methods section, lines 346–349).
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading and insightful comment, which
prompted this important clarification of our methods.
⚫ Why they added an additional polymer without explaining how they differentiate
between the protein and the polymer.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and important
comment.
The polymer referred to in this context is amphipol, a short-chain amphipathic
polymer widely used in structural biology to replace detergents at the transmembrane
surface of membrane proteins, thereby stabilizing their structure in aqueous
solution17,18. Amphipol is chemically distinct from silk fibroin and is known not to
form fibrillar or ordered structures on its own in solution.
Nonetheless, we fully agree with the reviewer that clearly distinguishing between
protein and polymer contributions in our data is essential for clarity. In response to
this concern, we have included additional metal shadowing electron microscopy
results in the revised manuscript (lines127-129, supplementary Fig. 1c-e) that
compare the morphology of samples with and without amphipol. These results show
that amphipol alone does not form any nanofibril structures under the experimental
conditions used (Fig. 1a), while NSF retains its characteristic nanofibrillar
morphology even in the absence of amphipol (Fig. 1b-c). Thus, the nanofibril
structures observed in our experiments can be confidently attributed to NSF and not to
amphipol.
Fig. 1 Effect of amphipol on the morphology of NSF. (a) Metal shadowing image of amphipol
alone (0.18 mg mL-1). (b) Metal shadowing image of NSF (0.03 mg mL-1) without amphipol. (c)
Metal shadowing image of NSF mixed with amphipol at a mass ratio of 1:6 in the extraction
buffer (50 mmol L−1 NaCl, 50 mmol L−1 Bis-Tris, 0.5 mmol L−1 EDTA, pH 7.5), with a final NSF
concentration of 0.03 mg mL−1. Scale bar: 200 nm.
The addition of amphipol in selected assays was motivated by its ability to stabilize
NSF under in vitro conditions, particularly during sample handling and preparation.
NSF is known to be highly unstable once extracted, and tends to aggregate or
precipitate rapidly—even at low temperatures and in the absence of freezing19-22. In
our previous work16, we performed extensive screening and found that both amphipol
and digitonin significantly enhance the solubility and stability of NSF (Fig. 2a-b).
Turbidity assays and circular dichroism (CD) analysis further confirmed that NSF
remained stable for at least 336 hours in the presence of digitonin (Fig. 2c-e).
Moreover, CD analysis showed that digitonin did not appreciably alter the random
coil structure of freshly extracted NSF (Fig. 2f). Although amphipol similarly
stabilizes NSF in solution, its high absorbance interferes with CD spectroscopy.
Reproduced from Song, K. et al. Decoding silkworm spinning programmed by pH and metal ions. Sci. Bull. 69, 792-802 (2024)
under CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
Fig. 2. Digitonin and Amphipol stabilized NSF in vitro. (a) A280 of NSF over time in the
presence of MSP1D1 or BSA. (b) A280 of NSF over time in the presence of detergents. (c)
NSF turbidity analysis. The inset (left) showed that NSF was stable in the presence of digitonin
after 336 h. The inset (right) showed the aggregation of NSF in the absence of digitonin after
336 h. (d) CD spectra of NSF in the presence of digitonin over time. (e) CD spectra of NSF in the
absence of digitonin over time. (f) CD spectra of NSF in the presence or absence of digitonin.
Taken together, these findings validate the use of amphipol and digitonin as essential
stabilizing agents that do not introduce structural artifacts or interfere with the
interpretation of NSF morphology. All structural analyses and tomographic
reconstructions were performed on samples in which amphipol was either excluded or
its influence empirically shown to be negligible.
We once again thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which helped us
significantly improve the clarity and rigor of our methodological description in the
revised manuscript.
⚫ Why they froze the entire silk gland and how they prevented ice nucleation in this
process.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and important
question.
The decision to freeze the entire silkworm was primarily based on practical
considerations. Rearing silkworms is time-consuming, as each lifecycle spans
approximately 60 days, and the availability of fresh mulberry leaves becomes highly
limited during the winter season. To ensure experimental continuity and access to NSF,
we opted to freeze whole silkworms and subsequently purify NSF from their silk
glands as needed, thereby eliminating the need for continuous rearing.
We acknowledge the general concern that freezing biological specimens may induce
irreversible structural changes, such as precipitation or denaturation. Indeed, previous
studies and our own observations indicate have shown that extracted NSF undergoes
irreversible precipitation when frozen in liquid nitrogen23,24, likely due to
shear-induced aggregation during the freeze-thaw cycle25,26. It is well known that
freezing and thawing induce regenerated silk fibroin (RSF) or NSF to form porous
structures in vitro27-29. However, it is important to emphasize that the solution
microenvironment of RSF or NSF in vitro differs significantly from its native
physiological environment within the silk gland lumen. The physiological conditions
inside the gland—including specific ion concentrations, pH, and potential stabilizing
biomolecules—appear to play a protective role in preserving the integrity of NSF
even under freezing conditions. Moreover, the intact silkworm body may further
buffer the silk gland against rapid temperature fluctuations and mechanical stress,
thereby reducing the likelihood of ice crystal-induced damage.
In support of this, our previous work16 demonstrated that soluble NSF could be
successfully extracted from silk glands of frozen silkworms (Fig. 1a-b), suggesting
that the physiological environment within the lumen of silk gland—including ions, pH,
and possibly unknown protective factors—may be essential roles in preventing NSF
denaturation or coagulation. Furthermore, SDS-PAGE analysis revealed that NSFs
purified from the posterior silk gland (PSG), the posterior region of middle silk gland
(PMSG), the middle region of middle silk gland (MMSG) and the anterior region of
middle silk gland (AMSG) of frozen silkworms exhibited identical electrophoretic
mobility and molecular composition as NSF extracted from the anterior silk gland
(ASG) of living silkworm (Fig. 1b-c).
Reproduced from Song, K. et al. Decoding silkworm spinning programmed by pH and metal ions. Sci. Bull. 69, 792-802 (2024) under CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
Fig. 1. Purification of NSF from silk gland. (a) Silk gland of the silkworm. The silk gland is
divided into ASG, MSG and PSG. MSG is further divided into AMSG, MMSG and PMSG. (b)
NSF was purified from PSG, AMSG, MMSG and PMSG of frozen silkworm, respectively, and
then separated by a linear 4%-16% gradient SDS-PAGE. (c) Top. A linear 4%-16% gradient
SDS-PAGE analysis of NSF purified by ions exchange chromatography. M, marker; CR, the crude
extraction of ASG of living silkworm; F1, the flow-through fraction after S cation exchange media;
S, cation exchange media; F2, the flow-through fraction after Q anion exchange media; Q, anion
exchange media. Bottom, NSF purified by size exclusion chromatography. The inset showed the
purity of NSF valued by 4%-16% SDS-PAGE. Fractions 1 and 2 were pooled for CD spectra and
metal shadowing, respectively.
Metal shadowing confirmed the formation of nanofibrils in all these samples, which
closely resembled those derived from living silkworms (Fig. 2a). In addition, circular
dichroism (CD) spectra revealed NSFs from PSG, PMSG, MMSG and AMSG of
frozen silkworms exhibited secondary structures comparable to those of NSF from
ASG of living silkworms (Fig. 2b).
Reproduced from Song, K. et al. Decoding silkworm spinning programmed by pH and metal ions. Sci. Bull. 69, 792-802 (2024) under CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
Fig. 2. The morphology and structure of NSF. (a) Metal shadowing of NSF from PSG, PMSG,
MMSG, AMSG of frozen silkworm and ASG of living silkworm. Scale bar, 200 nm. (b) CD
spectra of NSF from PSG, PMSG, MMSG, AMSG of frozen silkworm and ASG of living
silkworm.
Taken together, these results provide strong evidence that NSF extracted from frozen
silkworms retains its native morphology, molecular composition, and structural
features, thereby validating the use of frozen specimens in our study without
compromising the reliability of our findings. Once again, we sincerely appreciate the
reviewer’s insightful comments.
⚫ How they utilized FIB milling and managed to avoid graphitization, considering
that silk has low thermal conductivity and may burn even under cryo-FIB conditions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this very important and insightful question.
We fully acknowledge the potential concern that focused ion beam (FIB) milling,
even under cryogenic conditions, could induce structural alterations in sensitive
biological materials, particularly protein-based fibers. This issue was carefully
considered during our experimental design, especially regarding the reliability of
ultrastructural features observed in lamellae. However, although we lacked access to
advanced analytical tools (such as EDS) and knowledge reserves to directly evaluate
potential damage (e.g., carbonization) in lamellae, we performed structural
cross-validation using an independent experimental approach. Specifically, we
conducted single-particle cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and subtomogram
averaging on NSF extracted from silk gland that had not undergone FIB processing.
Remarkably, the basic structural units observed in the FIB-milled lamellae closely
matched those seen in the cryo-ET reconstructions from extracted NSF samples,
providing strong biochemical and morphological evidence that the ultrastructure
within the lamellae was well preserved and not artificially induced during FIB
milling.
Furthermore, as shown in Fig. 2a of the manuscript, the lamella included both
fibroin-rich and sericin-rich regions. Notably, the sericin-rich region (left side) lacked
nanofibrillar organization, while the fibroin-rich region (right side) displayed dense
nanofibrillar networks. Since sericin is a globular protein and is not naturally fibrillar,
the absence of nanofibrils in this region argues strongly against the possibility that
nanofibrils in the fibroin region are artifacts introduced by the FIB processing. This
internal spatial distinction within the same lamella supports the conclusion that the
nanofibrillar organization observed in the fibroin region is intrinsic and not
beam-induced.
Additionally, recent advances in cryo-FIB milling technology have demonstrated that,
when carefully implemented, this technique can preserve native biological structures
with high fidelity and has been widely used in in situ cryo-ET for cellular and
macromolecular imaging30-40.
In our study, we employed a state-of-the-art Thermo Fisher Helios NanoLab 600i
DualBeam cryo-FIB/SEM system specifically optimized for cryo-electron microscopy
sample preparation. Several key precautions were taken to minimize beam-induced
heating and structural damage:
Use of fresh, hydrated silk fibers:
The silk fibers used for cryo-FIB milling were freshly drawn from the silkworm
spinneret, and retained intrinsic moisture. The presence of water enhances local
electrical conductivity and thermal dissipation, significantly reducing sample charging
and heat accumulation during ion beam exposure. This moisture content helped
mitigate thermal damage and the risk of graphitization, in contrast to dried cocoon
silk.
Cryogenic conditions throughout the FIB process:
All FIB milling procedures were conducted under deep cryogenic conditions (< –
180 °C) using the Helios NanoLab system. At such low temperatures, biological
samples are vitrified, effectively preserving their native structures while dramatically
reducing thermal diffusion and decomposition. This approach effectively eliminates
the risk of burning or graphitization, even in materials with low thermal conductivity
like silk.
Triple-layer protective platinum coating:
Prior to milling, we deposited three successive layers of protective platinum (Pt) on
the fiber surface. These coatings:
· Enhanced surface conductivity,
· Provided shielding from direct ion beam exposure,
· Distributed both charge and heat more evenly,
· Prevented sputtering and beam-induced structural degradation.
Low current milling during final thinning steps:
For the final thinning of the lamellae, we employed extremely low ion beam currents
(10 pA) to minimize any residual heat generation. This is a widely accepted approach
in cryo-FIB protocols to prevent damage in sensitive specimens.
Collectively, these precautions ensured that sample preparation was conducted with
minimal physical or thermal disturbance. Most importantly, the consistent
morphological features observed between cryo-ET reconstructions from FIB-milled
lamellae and independently prepared NSF samples strongly supports the conclusion
that cryo-FIB milling did not introduce significant structural artifacts or thermal
damage in our study.
Once again, we sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this critical point, which has
helped us improve the rigor and clarity of our methodological description.
Co-reviewer
Overall, I find the paper interesting, and it is clear that significant work and effort
have gone into acquiring these results. It presents important findings regarding the
size and morphology of silk nanofibrils under different conditions. The use of FIB to
create lamellae for TEM imaging is a crucial point, as it emphasizes their effort to
maintain the native structure of silk fiber nanostructures.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive and encouraging
comments.
We are grateful that the reviewer found our study interesting and recognized the
significance of our findings regarding the size and morphology of silk nanofibrils. We
also greatly appreciate the acknowledgment of the substantial experimental effort
involved. These comments are highly motivating and have been instrumental in
helping us further refine and improve the manuscript.
However, I am not fully convinced that the results are reliable. The bottom line is that
they did not measure any material in its native state; they consistently altered it in
some way. Even the silk fibers used were forced reeled from the animal. Additional

demonstrate the reliability of our results. Specifically, we addressed three key steps
that may be viewed as perturbative:
Addition of amphipol to preserve NSF in solution:
The polymer referred to in this context is amphipol, a short-chain amphipathic

surface of membrane proteins, thereby stabilizing their structure in aqueous
solution17,18. Amphipol is chemically distinct from silk fibroin and is known not to
form fibrillar or ordered structures on its own in solution.
Nonetheless, we fully agree with the reviewer that clearly distinguishing between
protein and polymer contributions in our data is essential for clarity. In response to
this concern, we have included additional metal shadowing electron microscopy
results in the revised manuscript (lines127-129, supplementary Fig. 1c-e) that
compare the morphology of samples with and without amphipol. These results show

conditions used (Fig. 1a), while NSF retains its characteristic nanofibrillar
morphology even in the absence of amphipol (Fig. 1b-c). Thus, the nanofibril
structures observed in our experiments can be confidently attributed to NSF and not to
amphipol.

The decision to freeze the entire silkworm was primarily based on practical
considerations. Rearing silkworms is time-consuming, as each lifecycle spans
approximately 60 days, and the availability of fresh mulberry leaves becomes highly
limited during the winter season. To ensure experimental continuity and access to NSF,
we opted to freeze whole silkworms and subsequently purify NSF from their silk
glands as needed, thereby eliminating the need for continuous rearing.
We acknowledge the general concern that freezing biological specimens may induce
irreversible structural changes, such as precipitation or denaturation. Indeed, previous
studies and our own observations indicate have shown that extracted NSF undergoes
irreversible precipitation when frozen in liquid nitrogen23,24, likely due to
shear-induced aggregation during the freeze-thaw cycle25,26. It is well known that
freezing and thawing induce regenerated silk fibroin (RSF) or NSF to form porous
structures in vitro27-29. However, it is important to emphasize that the solution
microenvironment of RSF or NSF in vitro differs significantly from its native
physiological environment within the silk gland lumen. The physiological conditions
inside the gland—including specific ion concentrations, pH, and potential stabilizing
biomolecules—appear to play a protective role in preserving the integrity of NSF
even under freezing conditions. Moreover, the intact silkworm body may further
buffer the silk gland against rapid temperature fluctuations and mechanical stress,
thereby reducing the likelihood of ice crystal-induced damage.

successfully extracted from silk glands of frozen silkworms (Fig. 3a-b), suggesting

denaturation or coagulation. Furthermore, SDS-PAGE analysis revealed that NSFs
purified from the posterior silk gland (PSG), the posterior region of middle silk gland

middle silk gland (AMSG) of frozen silkworms exhibited identical electrophoretic
mobility and molecular composition as NSF extracted from the anterior silk gland
(ASG) of living silkworm (Fig. 3b-c).

Force-drawn fibers from silkworm and spider:
It is important to note that, in nature, both silkworm cocoon formation and spider web
weaving involve the natural pulling or drawing of silk proteins from the gland. The
natural spinning speeds are approximately 4-15 mm s-1 for silkworms and 10-20 mm
s-1 for spiders41. In our study, we carefully calibrated the forced reeling speed to fall
within these physiological ranges as closely as possible, thereby minimizing
mechanical stress and preserving native structural features.
To further confirm that forced reeling does not introduce structural artifacts, we also
performed cryo-FIB milling and cryo-electron tomography on silk fibers extracted
directly from silkworm cocoons. The lamellar ultrastructure of cocoon silk was
consistent with that observed in freshly drawn silk (Fig. 5), supporting the reliability
of our approach. However, due to pronounced image drift during tilt-series acquisition
of lamellae prepared from dried cocoon silk, we ultimately excluded these samples
from tomographic data collection. We speculate that this instability arose from the
complete dehydration of cocoon silk, which compromises its electrical conductivity.
The resulting charge accumulation during imaging likely caused the observed drift.
In contrast, freshly drawn silkworm silk and spider silk retain residual moisture,
which enhances conductivity and stabilizes imaging during cryo-ET. Thus, our choice
to use freshly reeled silks for tomographic analysis was driven primarily by their
superior performance under cryo-imaging conditions.

here are reliable and faithfully reflect native silk protein assemblies.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this very important and insightful question.
We fully acknowledge the potential concern that focused ion beam (FIB) milling,
even under cryogenic conditions, could induce structural alterations in sensitive
biological materials, particularly protein-based fibers. This issue was carefully
considered during our experimental design, especially regarding the reliability of
ultrastructural features observed in lamellae. However, although we lacked access to
advanced analytical tools (such as EDS) and knowledge reserves to directly evaluate
potential damage (e.g., carbonization) in lamellae, we performed structural
cross-validation using an independent experimental approach. Specifically, we
conducted single-particle cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and subtomogram
averaging on NSF extracted from silk gland that had not undergone FIB processing.
Remarkably, the basic structural units observed in the FIB-milled lamellae closely
matched those seen in the cryo-ET reconstructions from extracted NSF samples,
providing strong biochemical and morphological evidence that the ultrastructure
within the lamellae was well preserved and not artificially induced during FIB
milling.
Furthermore, as shown in Fig. 2a of the manuscript, the lamella included both
fibroin-rich and sericin-rich regions. Notably, the sericin-rich region (left side) lacked
nanofibrillar organization, while the fibroin-rich region (right side) displayed dense
nanofibrillar networks. Since sericin is a globular protein and is not naturally fibrillar,
the absence of nanofibrils in this region argues strongly against the possibility that
nanofibrils in the fibroin region are artifacts introduced by the FIB processing. This
internal spatial distinction within the same lamella supports the conclusion that the
nanofibrillar organization observed in the fibroin region is intrinsic and not
beam-induced.
Additionally, recent advances in cryo-FIB milling technology have demonstrated that,
when carefully implemented, this technique can preserve native biological structures
with high fidelity and has been widely used in in situ cryo-ET for cellular and
macromolecular imaging30-40.
In our study, we employed a state-of-the-art Thermo Fisher Helios NanoLab 600i
DualBeam cryo-FIB/SEM system specifically optimized for cryo-electron microscopy
sample preparation. Several key precautions were taken to minimize beam-induced
heating and structural damage:
Use of fresh, hydrated silk fibers:
The silk fibers used for cryo-FIB milling were freshly drawn from the silkworm
spinneret, and retained intrinsic moisture. The presence of water enhances local
electrical conductivity and thermal dissipation, significantly reducing sample charging
and heat accumulation during ion beam exposure. This moisture content helped
mitigate thermal damage and the risk of graphitization, in contrast to dried cocoon
silk.
Cryogenic conditions throughout the FIB process:
All FIB milling procedures were conducted under deep cryogenic conditions (< –
180 °C) using the Helios NanoLab system. At such low temperatures, biological
samples are vitrified, effectively preserving their native structures while dramatically
reducing thermal diffusion and decomposition. This approach effectively eliminates
the risk of burning or graphitization, even in materials with low thermal conductivity
like silk.
Triple-layer protective platinum coating:
Prior to milling, we deposited three successive layers of protective platinum (Pt) on
the fiber surface. These coatings:
· Enhanced surface conductivity,
· Provided shielding from direct ion beam exposure,
· Distributed both charge and heat more evenly,
· Prevented sputtering and beam-induced structural degradation.
Low current milling during final thinning steps:
For the final thinning of the lamellae, we employed extremely low ion beam currents
(10 pA) to minimize any residual heat generation. This is a widely accepted approach
in cryo-FIB protocols to prevent damage in sensitive specimens.
Collectively, these precautions ensured that sample preparation was conducted with
minimal physical or thermal disturbance. Most importantly, the consistent
morphological features observed between cryo-ET reconstructions from FIB-milled
lamellae and independently prepared NSF samples strongly supports the conclusion
that cryo-FIB milling did not introduce significant structural artifacts or thermal
damage in our study.
Once again, we sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this critical point, which has
helped us improve the rigor and clarity of our methodological description.
